summary:
Uttar Pradesh stands under India's national framework for transgender persons. India's Parliament passed the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill in March 2026, replacing the 2019 law's self-identification route with legal recognition limited to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner, and to intersex individuals. Trans men, trans women and non-binary people who self-identify outside those categories fall outside the recognition scheme. Rights activists, among them Akkai Padmashali, describe the amendment as criminalising and an attack on the right to exist. The government presents it as widening access to welfare schemes and protection from trafficking; critics say it excludes many trans, non-binary and gender-fluid people. India has an estimated two million transgender people.

The baseline for entry and stay is mixed. Same-sex acts were decriminalised by the Supreme Court in 2018, and discrimination is barred on grounds including sex, which the Supreme Court has held covers sexual orientation and gender identity under Article 15; the Allahabad High Court extended that in 2021 to bar employment discrimination on sexual orientation grounds. There is no same-sex marriage or civil partnership, although courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units.

Criminal-law protection weakened in 2024. Replacing the Indian Penal Code with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita removed legal safeguards that had protected trans persons from sexual violence, and trans people fear a rise in assaults because the new code omits the gender-identity-specific offences the old law carried.

Identity documents remain a live source of friction. In February 2026 the Allahabad High Court granted relief to a trans person who had been asked to take a medical exam by passport authorities, indicating that intrusive document screening has been applied to trans travellers in Uttar Pradesh and that the state's high court has intervened against it.

The most trans-visible public space in Uttar Pradesh is the Maha Kumbh gathering in Prayagraj. On 12 February 2025, at the fourth ceremonial bath of the 45-day fair, Pavitra Nandagiri, a Mahamandaleshwar of the Kinnar Akhada and one of the gathering's highest-ranking monks, led 15 transgender spiritual leaders in the ritual bathing, marching alongside Naga Sadhus and Aghori. The episode documents an institutionalised trans religious hierarchy operating openly in the state.

Trans-specific violence is documented. Kajal, a 25-year-old transgender woman in Kanpur, was killed in a home-invasion robbery; the record dates to 10 August 2025, a suspect was later arrested, and her 12-year-old adopted brother also died. The killing was logged in the 2025 international transgender day of remembrance list through local press reporting.

Protection machinery at state level is mandated but its Uttar Pradesh implementation is not established in the sources. The Ministry of Social Justice stated on 8 December 2021 that state governments must constitute Transgender Welfare Boards under section 10(1) of the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Rules, 2020, and all state governments were reminded on 9 October 2020 to act.

Assessments of police conduct diverge. The United Kingdom's December 2025 country policy note records limited reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic; victim interviews documented in June 2024 record abusive treatment of trans detainees by railway police.
tangentialFactors:
Checkpoint friction against trans people is recorded elsewhere in India and shapes what a visitor may face in transit. In November 2024 an openly transgender law student, Sakshi Jain, was stopped at Chennai International Airport Terminal 1 by Central Industrial Security Force personnel despite presenting her PAN card for identity verification. In Kolkata a transwoman alleged that a Railway Protection Force constable groped her at the station under the pretext of checking her gender, and transgender persons arrested by the Railway Protection Force in Assam have recounted degrading treatment in custody.

Facilities and welfare coordination are largely set at state level, and Uttar Pradesh is not among the states named as running such machinery. Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Maharashtra and Odisha run transgender welfare boards coordinating housing subsidies, free sex reassignment surgery in public hospitals and pensions, and several states provide targeted welfare, housing and healthcare benefits for hijras.

Judicial protection elsewhere in India is stronger than the national picture suggests. The Madras High Court's judgment of 7 June 2021 in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police issued sweeping guidelines on protecting LGBTQIA+ persons, police sensitisation and a ban on conversion therapy, with directions to the National Medical Commission and education authorities. Bans on conversion therapy from that judgment and from the National Medical Commission in 2022 coexist with clandestine networks still operating.

Intersex minors remain at risk nationally: reports document a history of infanticide and a strong parental preference for assigning intersex infants male through non-consensual operations, and the Madras High Court ordered Tamil Nadu in April 2019 to ban sex-selective surgeries on intersex infants. No equivalent Uttar Pradesh order is sourced.
localsOnly:
The Ayushman Bharat scheme was expanded in April 2024 to cover transition-related healthcare for all members of the transgender community, a resident-facing entitlement rather than a visitor benefit.

In August 2024 the Ministry of Finance clarified that LGBTQ people face no restrictions on opening joint bank accounts or naming partners as beneficiaries.

Residents can invoke section 10(1) of the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Rules, 2020 to demand that the state government constitute a Transgender Welfare Board; the Ministry of Social Justice issued that reading on 8 December 2021 after reminding all state governments on 9 October 2020.

Transgender religious office-holding is an established local institution: the Kinnar Akhada at the Prayagraj Maha Kumbh is headed by a Mahamandaleshwar, a rank held by Pavitra Nandagiri, and transgender spiritual leaders take part in the ceremonial baths as a matter of ritual protocol.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether Uttar Pradesh has in fact constituted a Transgender Welfare Board under section 10(1) is unresolved in the sources; only the national obligation and the 2020 and 2021 reminders are documented.

Enforcement practice in Uttar Pradesh under the March 2026 amendment is not sourced: no arrests, prosecutions or administrative refusals under the narrowed recognition scheme are recorded here.

The outcome of the Kajal case beyond the arrest of a suspect is unresolved; no charging or judicial result is sourced.

Whether the February 2026 Allahabad High Court relief produced a change in passport-authority screening practice for trans applicants is not sourced.

State-level welfare provision in Uttar Pradesh, including any housing subsidy, pension or surgery entitlement, is not sourced.
